structure: Hierarchical joint law with one plug-in parameter set. (1) Sex is Bernoulli. (2) Age is 18 plus a Gamma variate truncated at 90, independent of sex. (3) BMI is lognormal given sex and age, truncated to [13, 45]. (4) HDL and non-HDL cholesterol each have a raw-scale conditional mean that is exactly linear in the requested design columns [1, (age-50)/10, female, (bmi-25)/5]. Their errors are homoscedastic, right-skewed standardized shifted-lognormal variates, independent of the covariates, coupled by a Gaussian copula. (5) Total cholesterol is HDL plus non-HDL, so TC exceeds HDL and all lipids are positive by construction. Because the conditional means are linear and the error covariance is constant, the population OLS coefficients equal the structural coefficients and the population residual correlation equals the error correlation, whatever the covariate mixture. Source confidence intervals were used only to judge the scale of reported slopes, never as individual dispersion. Parameter uncertainty is not propagated into the cohort; sensitivity ranges are given under limitations. All values are transported from Malawi, Uganda and Ghana summaries to the Turkana context by explicit assumption.

Moving to BMI 25 with the BMI slope gives 1.06. Age: 0.0 per decade, an explicit assumption because no HDL-age statistic is supplied. Female: within-stratum Greiner female-minus-male differences of 0.05, 0.05 and 0.09, plus about 0.01 for higher female BMI, give 0.07. Unadjusted or age/smoking/alcohol-adjusted source slopes are taken to approximate the age/sex-adjusted slope. A common BMI slope across sexes deliberately omits a sex-by-BMI interaction. parameter_provenance.meaning_operator: Coefficients of E[non-HDL | age, sex, BMI] on the same design; the TC coefficients are the element-wise sum with lipids.hdl.coef

The chosen TC slope is 0.05 per kg/m^2, i.e. 0.25 per 5 kg/m^2, so the non-HDL slope is 0.25 - (-0.0275) = 0.2775. Intercept: n-weighted Greiner male non-HDL geometric mean of about 2.50, times about 1.04, gives about 2.60 at age near 32 and BMI near 21.6. The age slope is not identified by the supplied evidence. Common BMI slope across sexes. Assay, fasting and population transfer. A geometric-mean difference is not a difference of geometric means; it is used only as an approximate level guide.

parameter_provenance.meaning_operator: Shape s of the standardized shifted-lognormal error (exp(s*z) - exp(s^2/2)) / sqrt((exp(s^2)-1)*exp(s^2)); sets right skew and the lower bound -1/sqrt(exp(s^2)-1)

requested_estimands.derivation: E[HDL | age, sex, BMI] is exactly linear in the requested design, with errors independent of covariates. The population OLS coefficient on (bmi-25)/5 is therefore lipids.hdl.coef[3] = -0.0275 mmol/L. Multiplying by 38.67 gives -1.063425. This is a model-implied population value, not a simulated-sample estimate; finite samples will vary around it.
TC = HDL + non-HDL, so the population OLS coefficient on (bmi-25)/5 is -0.0275 + 0.2775 = 0.25 mmol/L. Multiplying by 38.67 gives 9.6675.

With linear means and a constant error covariance independent of covariates, the population residuals equal the structural errors. Corr(e_TC, e_HDL) = (sH^2 + rho*sH*sN) / (sH*sqrt(sH^2 + sN^2 + 2*rho*sH*sN)), with sH = 0.33, sN = 0.80 and rho = 0. This gives 0.33/sqrt(0.7489), approximately 0.381331. The value is unit-invariant.

limitations: No Turkana data or target statistics were used. Lipid levels, slopes, dispersion and correlation are transported from Malawi, Uganda and Ghana summaries with different assays (laboratory enzymatic vs CardioChek Plus on venous EDTA), fasting protocols, health exclusions, age ranges and lifestyles. Unit conversion does not establish assay equivalence.

Target covariate composition (age, sex, BMI, site and lifestyle mixture) is unspecified and assumed. No mixture components for pastoralist vs urban lifestyle or Turkana vs Laikipia sites are modelled. The requested estimands are invariant to covariate composition only because exact linearity, homoscedasticity and a common BMI slope across sexes were assumed.

Source regression scales are ambiguous: Agongo log base is unspecified and Greiner response and predictor transforms are unresolved. Natural-log and raw-scale readings were adopted by assumption. Source adjustment sets (none, or age/smoking/alcohol) differ from the requested age/sex/BMI set.
Obirikorang statistics are unadjusted Spearman correlations and conflict with the Greiner-based HDL/non-HDL association. The chosen residual correlation is a judgment compromise.

Plausible sensitivity ranges from the bridges, not confidence intervals: HDL-BMI about -1.5 to -0.8 mg/dL per 5 kg/m^2; TC-BMI about 8 to 13 mg/dL per 5 kg/m^2; residual TC-HDL correlation about 0.15 to 0.46.

Parameter uncertainty is not propagated into the cohort; one plug-in law is used. Source confidence intervals were not converted to individual SDs. The quarantined Malawi urban women HDL interval and the rounded or collapsed intervals were not used.

Repeated summaries from one source cohort (Greiner strata and regressions, Agongo tables, Obirikorang pairs) are dependent evidence and were not treated as independent replications. No inverse-variance weighting was performed.

Distribution shapes (gamma age, lognormal BMI, shifted-lognormal lipid errors) and support bounds (age up to 90, BMI 13-45) are assumptions. Age is continuous rather than integer. No measurement-range censoring, heteroscedasticity, sex-specific slopes or nonlinear age or BMI effects are included.
The HDL-age coefficient (0) and the non-HDL-age coefficient (0.08 mmol/L per decade) are not identified by the supplied evidence and are explicit assumptions.
Outputs are descriptive association projections of the generated law, not causal effects. Curator extractions were not re-authenticated against the original articles.
